newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire's Mobutu gives up power, keeps title.
newsitem.headline: Zaire's Mobutu gives up power, keeps title.

text.p: Zaire's ailing president, Mobutu Sese Seko, gave up power and left the capital, Kinshasa, Friday, ending over three decades of highly personalized rule over Africa's third largest nation.
A government statement said that the veteran leader, fighting cancer and seven months of civil war, would retain the title of president.
In Washington, U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright told reporters, "We believe that his departure now opens the way for a peaceful resolution of the military conflict."
Laurent Kabila's rebels, who control three-quarters of the shattered, corruption-plagued nation, had yet to comment.
Government spokesman Kin-Kiey Mulumba announced the news after Mobutu left for his northern jungle palace at Gbadolite, triggering intense speculation that he was going into exile.
"The president ... has ceased all intervention in the affairs of the state," Kin-Kiey told a news conference.
Speaking after a cabinet meeting, he said Mobutu's emergency rule prime minister, Gen. Likulia Bolongo, was in charge.
Kisangani Archbishop Laurent Monsengwo, a key player early in Zaire's attempts at democratic transition, would negotiate with Kabila's rebels on a new transitional government and elections.
Zaire's transitional constitution, he said, permitted Mobutu to step aside without actually resigning as president.

"If the parties to the conflict, in particular the rebel alliance, act in good faith, the president's important decision to stand aside, coupled with the constraints which the constitution imposes ... will allow us to find a satisfactory compromise between the positions of the belligerents," he said.
Sources in South Africa, whose president Nelson Mandela has been trying to broker a peaceful handover of power in Zaire, expressed initial surprise at Mobutu's handover of power.

Government sources said Mobutu had not discussed the move with Mandela, and a source close to the South African negotiating team said the announcement "does not fit any of the proposals on the table."

Zaire state television said Mobutu had gone to his stronghold home region of Gbadolite on doctor's orders. "The president of the republic went to Gbadolite this morning. He will take a few days of rest on the advice of his doctors."
Political and diplomatic sources said earlier that army chiefs had told him they could not defend the capital against the rebels and that he should leave for his own safety.
A Western diplomat in Morocco said Mobutu was expected there in the next 48 hours. "It seems that he has chosen Morocco as a place for exile," the diplomat said.
"I am hearing that Morocco is a likely first stop, with France as a final destination," one Western diplomat in Paris said. France declined all comment.
Prior to the statement on the handover of power, one source close to Mandela's negotiating team said reports that Mobutu was heading for France were more in line with expectations.
"We don't have any clarity on whether he is leaving for good. He has not said that to us," the source added.
Mandela's plan for a constitutional transition depended on Mobutu resigning formally, he added.
A close Mobutu relative said that members of Mobutu's entourage were told Thursday night to pack their bags and be ready to leave Kinshasa by dawn Friday morning.
Kabila left for rebel headquarters in the southern city of Lubumbashi after talks Thursday in South Africa with Mandela.
Kabila agreed to a request from Mandela to give Mobutu until Monday to study proposals for a peaceful handover of power.
Asked earlier if he would halt the rebel advance on Kinshasa, Kabila replied, "I have nothing to say about it."

Mobutu, 66, who is reputed to have amassed a huge personal fortune over the years, seized power in 1965. Western powers, ignoring the corruption of his dictatorial rule, supported him as a Cold War bastion against Soviet communism.
Kabila, 56, and his rebels took up arms in October in a dispute over Zairian nationality for ethnic Tutsis who had lived in eastern Zaire for generations.
Kinshasa, a teeming city of five million people, spent its third night under curfew but a semblance of normality returned Friday on news that Mobutu was studying the peace proposal.
Mobutu had agreed to hand over to an elected successor. Kabila demanded an immediate transfer of power to his alliance.
Mandela has been trying to avert a battle for Kinshasa but many residents were more afraid of a looting rampage by soldiers of Mobutu's notoriously ill-disciplined army.
Many had feared the worst Thursday after the collapse Wednesday of efforts by Mandela to bring Mobutu and Kabila together on a South African ship in Congo's main port.
As reports of Mobutu's departure spread through the streets, opponents expressed cautious satisfaction.
"We are waiting now for Kabila. We hope there has been an agreement to avoid bloodshed," Blaise Bomba, a member of the unofficial opposition "street parliament," said.
